question: Analyse, using Newton's First and Second Laws of motion, how a hockey player will move towards the ball from a stationary position.
markScheme:
4 marks from:
First Law:
- The hockey player provides force by contracting their leg muscles (1), using this force to overcome inertia, allowing them to move from a stationary position (1).
Second Law:
- By varying the force of muscular contraction/the number of motor units recruited, the player can cause a change in momentum from stationary to moving (1); the greater the force generated, the greater the acceleration towards the ball (1).

Time (s) | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6
Velocity (m/s) | 0 | 6 | 8 | 8.5 | 9 | 9.3 | 9.2

Identify the period of time when acceleration was the greatest.

During a badminton rally, players move quickly around the court to reach the shuttlecock.

Using Newton's Laws of Motion, explain how a player moves towards the shuttlecock during a rally.
markScheme:
Indicative content — mark using levels of response. Laws must be correctly identified to be credited.
- Force is applied by muscular contraction.
- Newton's First Law of Motion (law of inertia): the performer remains stationary unless a force is applied, to overcome the state of inertia.
- The performer continues to move towards the shuttlecock with constant velocity until another force is applied; muscles acting as a brake slow the performer to change direction/stop.
- Newton's Second Law of Motion (law of acceleration): Force = Mass x Acceleration; the mass of the performer is constant; the greater the force exerted on the ground (ground reaction force), the greater the acceleration/momentum towards the shuttlecock; force governs direction.
- Newton's Third Law (law of action and reaction): for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction; the force applied to the ground by the player generates an equal and opposite ground reaction force that moves the performer.
Max 8 marks.

question:
A water skier must generate a powerful initial force to rise out of the water at the start of a run.

Using Newton's First and Second Laws of Motion, explain how the water skier is able to rise up out of the water.
markScheme:
4 marks from:
- Force is applied by the muscles (sub max 2 marks).
- Newton's First Law of Motion/Law of Inertia: the skier will remain in the water unless a force is applied; the skier continues to move with constant velocity once up and planing, until another force is applied; the water/drag slows the skier.
- Newton's Second Law of Motion/Law of Acceleration: the mass of the skier is constant; the greater the force exerted (through the tow rope/against the water via the skis), the greater the acceleration/momentum; force governs direction.
Max 4 marks.

question: Which one of these measurements is a vector quantity?

A sports scientist records three force-time (impulse) graphs of a swimmer performing a tumble turn push-off, at different stages: the initial contact with the wall, mid push-off, and the moment of leaving the wall.

Graph P shows a large positive area under the curve with a short, sharp peak. Graph Q shows a small, roughly balanced area with minimal net force. Graph R shows a gradually building positive force that tails off smoothly as contact ends.

Identify which graph is most likely to represent the peak drive phase of the push-off, and justify your answer.
markScheme:
3 marks from:
- Graph P is most likely to represent the peak drive phase of the push-off.
- This is because a large positive impulse (large area under the curve, sharp peak of force) indicates a strong net force being applied to accelerate the swimmer away from the wall.
- The swimmer needs to generate maximum force in a short time to leave the wall with high velocity, consistent with a large, brief positive impulse.
Max 3 marks.

question:
It is important for competitive swimmers to push off the starting blocks effectively to achieve a fast dive start.

Using Newton's first and second laws of linear motion and knowledge of the neuromuscular system, analyse how a swimmer is able to achieve a fast, powerful start.

(AO1 = 2 marks, AO2 = 3 marks, AO3 = 3 marks)
markScheme:
Indicative content — mark holistically using the levels below.
AO1 may include: Newton's first law (law of inertia) — a body remains at rest or in uniform motion unless acted on by a force; Newton's second law (law of acceleration) — force = mass x acceleration, and the rate of change of momentum is proportional to the applied force, acting in the direction of that force. Neuromuscular system: muscle fibre types (Type I, IIa, IIx); spatial summation (varying the number/size of motor units recruited); wave summation (repeated impulses with insufficient time to relax, producing a tetanic contraction); all-or-none law within a motor unit.
AO2 may include: the swimmer's initial state of inertia is stationary on the blocks; a muscular force must be generated (leg extension/drive) to overcome this inertia and propel the body forward and downward off the blocks; varying the force of contraction and number of motor units recruited changes momentum from stationary to moving; recruiting a high proportion of fast twitch (Type IIx) fibres and large motor units generates the explosive force needed.
AO3 may include: the greater the force applied against the blocks, the greater the resulting acceleration (Newton's second law), giving the swimmer an advantage over competitors; if the swimmer increases the frequency of neural stimulation before the muscle fully relaxes (wave summation), a greater sustained force is produced, further increasing acceleration off the blocks.
Band 4 (7-8): Detailed, accurate, well-linked analysis across AO1/AO2/AO3.
Band 3 (5-6): Good knowledge and mostly accurate application/analysis.
Band 2 (3-4): Basic knowledge, limited application/analysis.
Band 1 (1-2): Very limited/isolated points.
0 marks: No relevant content.
Max 8 marks.

question:
A long jumper's horizontal velocity is recorded throughout their run-up, take-off and landing.

Analyse and suggest what impulse would be produced by the long jumper when:
- they begin their run-up from a stationary start
- they are sprinting at a constant pace during the middle of the run-up
- they make contact with the take-off board.

Justify your answers.

(AO1 = 4 marks, AO2 = 5 marks, AO3 = 6 marks)
markScheme:
Indicative content — mark holistically using the levels below.
AO1 may include: an impulse is the change of momentum of an object caused by a force acting over a time interval; impulse = force x time, often represented as a force-time graph, with time on the x-axis and force on the y-axis; graphs show negative and positive components of force.
AO2 may include: at the start of the run-up, net impulse is positive (the jumper accelerates from stationary); during the middle of the run-up at constant pace, positive and negative impulses are roughly equal, giving a net impulse of approximately zero (no further acceleration); at the take-off board, a large net impulse is generated (a strong vertical/forward force applied over a short time) to convert horizontal velocity into a combination of continued horizontal and new vertical momentum for flight.
AO3 may include: justification that a positive net impulse must exceed the negative/braking impulse for acceleration to occur at the start; that a stable/constant running speed requires the propulsive and braking impulses at each stride to balance; that at take-off, the jumper actively increases the force applied to the board (and the board's reaction force) over the brief ground contact time to generate the necessary vertical impulse for height, while trying to minimise the loss of horizontal speed.
Band 5 (13-15): Comprehensive, accurate, well-justified analysis across all three phases.
Band 4 (10-12): Good detail, mostly accurate, minor gaps.
Band 3 (7-9): Reasonable coverage of at least two phases, some justification.
Band 2 (4-6): Basic/limited knowledge and application.
Band 1 (1-3): Fragmented/isolated points.
0 marks: No relevant content.
Max 15 marks.
